160: I know the story of every object here. Long stories. I tell them at parties. Invitations are rare.
161: I can tell you where each piece came from and how old it is. My own age I keep politely vague.
162: Forty years I have cared for this collection. It has never been smaller than it is right now.
163: I know these objects like family. And like family, one of them has quietly slipped out.
164: Ask me anything about this collection. Anything at all. Just not about that empty shelf.
165: I chose every object here myself. I did not choose for one of them to go for a walk.
166: I've catalogued each piece down to the smallest scratch. My own handwriting is the true mystery.
167: My whole life is knowing where things belong. A spot on the wall now firmly disagrees.
168: I could recite this collection from memory. I'll skip one item, for reasons we won't discuss.
169: Every object here has a story. One of them, it turns out, has an ending I didn't write.
170: I labeled every case in this building. One label now describes a very tidy empty box.
171: I know the age of every treasure here to the year. And the exact minute one of them left.
172: People call me the keeper of the collection. Today I kept most of it. Most is a strong word.
173: I've dusted these shelves for decades. There is one shelf now that dusts unusually fast.
174: I remember when each piece arrived. Some came by ship, some by truck, one in a sad little envelope.
175: I wrote the book on this collection. I may need to add a short, sad new chapter.
176: I can find any object here with my eyes shut. My glasses, however, defeat me every single morning.
177: The collection is my life's work. Today my life's work has a small, cool breeze through it.
178: I know every piece so well I could draw them. My drawings resemble potatoes. Very old potatoes.
179: A child asked where the golden mask went. I, the expert, said the one thing experts dread: hm.
180: I serve food all day. Kings and rascals, same manners, same complaint: too slow.
181: Everyone at every table wants their meal faster. I have not yet learned to walk through walls.
182: I've served the rich and the rude. They order differently. They complain identically.
183: My job is carrying plates and smiling. The plates are heavy. The smiling is heavier.
184: A very important guest sent back the soup. It was, he said, too warm. It is soup.
185: I remember every order but never my own dinner, which I eat standing up at midnight.
186: I've balanced eleven plates on two arms. Nobody claps. They just ask for more bread.
187: Kings, thieves, everyone leaves the same tip. Which is to say, we don't talk about tips.
188: I carry hot food across a crowded room without spilling. It is my one great talent. Truly.
189: Someone ordered the chef's finest dish, then removed half the ingredients. Same as ever.
190: I hear every complaint in the world at these tables. My reply is always the same warm nod.
191: I've served people who own castles. They still ask if the water is free. It is.
192: My feet have walked a hundred miles between the kitchen and table four. Table four is fussy.
193: A grand guest snapped his fingers at me. I came. That is the job. The fingers, though.
194: Everyone wants the window seat. I do not control the windows. I've explained this often.
195: I refill water glasses all evening. Fill, empty, fill. It is the tide, but indoors.
196: One guest ordered the costly dish, then asked why it was so small. It is costly because it is small.
197: I've memorized the whole menu. Guests still ask what is good. Everything. It's all good.
198: I smile at every table, even the loud one. Especially the loud one. That is the real work.
199: I bring the food, I take the plates, I never sit. My chair at home barely knows me.
